facts.statehood_note: One of the original 13 states; this is the date Connecticut ratified the U.S. Constitution, the fifth state to do so.
facts.nickname: The Constitution State (official); also the Nutmeg State
facts.motto: Qui transtulit sustinet (Latin: He who transplanted still sustains)

symbols.name: Sperm whale (1975), chosen for Connecticut's whaling history and because it is endangered

facts.name_origin: From a Mohegan-Pequot word translated as "long tidal river" or "upon the long river," meaning the Connecticut River.

government.chambers: Connecticut State Senate (36 senators) and Connecticut House of Representatives (151 representatives)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term). The governor leads the executive branch. Voters also elect a lieutenant governor, secretary of the state, treasurer, comptroller and attorney general every four years.
government.courts: Connecticut Supreme Court (7 justices: a chief justice and six associate justices, who sit in Hartford across from the State Capitol). Below it are the Appellate Court and the Superior Court.
government.local: Connecticut has 169 towns, and towns do most local governing. The state has 8 counties, but county governments were mostly ended in 1960; the counties are now used for maps and weather reports. Nine regional councils of governments help towns plan together.
government.constitution: The current constitution was adopted in 1965, replacing the constitution of 1818. Before that, Connecticut was governed by the Fundamental Orders (adopted January 14, 1639) and the Charter of 1662.
government.kid_line: "No person shall be denied the equal protection of the law nor be subjected to segregation or discrimination in the exercise or enjoyment of his or her civil or political rights because of religion, race, color, ancestry, national origin, sex or physical or mental disability." (Connecticut Constitution, Article First, Section 20, as amended in 1984)

long_ago.about: In the early 1600s about 8,000 Pequot people lived in southeastern Connecticut between the Thames and Pawcatuck rivers. They hunted, gathered shellfish and grew corn, beans and squash planted together, and a smallpox epidemic in 1633–1634 killed about half of them.

About 1,500 to 2,500 Mohegan people lived west of the Thames River. Their sachem Uncas settled them on the west bank of the river, which they call the Massapequotuck, and it became a center for making and trading wampum.

long_ago.nation: The River nations (including the Tunxis, Podunk, Wangunk, Hammonasset, Quinnipiac and Schaghticoke)
long_ago.about: Many Algonquian-speaking communities, often grouped together as the River nations, lived in the Connecticut region. People moved with the seasons to use different foods and resources.
The Paugussett are one of the nations that still live in Connecticut; today the Golden Hill Paugussett keep reservation land in Trumbull and Colchester.
Nipmuc homelands reached into northeastern Connecticut. Today the Nipmuc are based in a neighboring state, but Connecticut is part of their homeland.

today.about: Federally recognized in 1983 and state recognized; its reservation is one of the longest continually lived-on reservations in North America, and it runs the Mashantucket Pequot Museum and Research Center.
Federally recognized in 1994 and state recognized; it runs the Tantaquidgeon Museum in Uncasville and bought back its Fort Shantok land in 1995.
State recognized, with a reservation in North Stonington, one of the oldest continuously lived-on reservations in the country.
State recognized, with a reservation of about 300 acres in Kent, west of the Housatonic River.
State recognized, with two reservations in Trumbull and Colchester.

first_peoples.today_note: Connecticut has five state-recognized tribal nations. Two of them, the Mashantucket Pequot and the Mohegan, are also federally recognized. Some nations with homelands in Connecticut, such as the Nipmuc and Narragansett, are based in neighboring states today.
sites: Mashantucket Pequot Museum and Research Center (Mashantucket)
Tantaquidgeon Museum, Uncasville (opened in 1931; the oldest museum owned and run by Native people in the United States)
Fort Shantok, the Mohegan homeland on the Thames River where Uncas settled his people

history.event: Indigenous Peoples are living in the Connecticut region, using stone tools to hunt, fish and work wood and moving with the seasons.
Pequot, Mohegan and other Algonquian-speaking nations farm corn, beans and squash together, gather shellfish, and use wampum made from quahog and whelk shells as money and as a record of agreements.
Dutch explorer Adriaen Block explores the region. Dutch traders later build a fort called the House of Hope at Hartford.
English Puritans led by Thomas Hooker come from Massachusetts and start the Connecticut Colony at Hartford, on Indigenous land.

Connecticut Colony declares war on the Pequot on May 1. On May 26, colonists and their Mohegan and Narragansett allies burn the Pequot fort near the Mystic River and kill hundreds of Pequot people. Many Pequot captives are enslaved.

The Pequot War ends with the Treaty of Hartford, which splits the surviving Pequot among the Mohegan and Narragansett and forbids them to call themselves Pequot. The Pequot keep their identity anyway.
On January 14, the Connecticut General Court adopts the Fundamental Orders, a written plan of government for the river towns.
King Charles II grants a charter that unites Connecticut's settlements.
A gradual emancipation law says children born to enslaved mothers after March 1, 1784, will be freed only when they grow up. It frees no one already enslaved.
On January 9, Connecticut ratifies the U.S. Constitution and becomes the fifth state.
Prudence Crandall opens her Canterbury school to Black girls and young women. The General Assembly passes the "Black Law" to stop her, and she is arrested.
Africans who took over the slave ship La Amistad are jailed in New Haven. Their case goes to the U.S. Supreme Court, which rules for them on March 9, 1841, and 35 return home to Sierra Leone.

On April 3, soldiers of the 29th Connecticut (Colored) Infantry are among the first Union infantry to enter Richmond, Virginia, the Confederate capital. Connecticut sent about 55,000 men to fight for the Union.

trailblazers.name: Samson Occom
trailblazers.text: Born near New London, he learned Latin, Greek and Hebrew and became a minister. From 1766 to 1767 he preached more than 300 sermons across Britain and raised over 12,000 pounds for a school, and he was the first Native American to write down his own life story. He helped found the community that became the Brothertown Indians.

trailblazers.name: Venture Smith
trailblazers.text: Born Broteer in West Africa, he was captured as a boy and enslaved in Connecticut and New York. He worked extra jobs, such as cutting wood, to buy his own freedom, then worked to reunite his family and built a farm of more than 100 acres at Haddam Neck. His life story, published in New London in 1798, is one of the very few firsthand accounts by a captive carried across the Atlantic.

trailblazers.name: Prudence Crandall and Sarah Harris
trailblazers.group: White Quaker teacher and Black American student
trailblazers.text: In 1832 Prudence Crandall let Sarah Harris, a 20-year-old Black woman who wanted to be a teacher, into her Canterbury school. When white families pulled their daughters out, Crandall opened the school to Black girls instead. A mob attacked the school and she was jailed under the 1833 "Black Law," and in 1995 she was named Connecticut's State Heroine.

trailblazers.name: Sengbe Pieh (Joseph Cinqué)
trailblazers.group: West African freedom fighter from Sierra Leone
trailblazers.text: Kidnapped from Sierra Leone and sold in Cuba, he led the captives' revolt aboard La Amistad in 1839. The Africans were jailed in New Haven, and their case reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which freed them in 1841. He wrote to the President, "We want to go home," and he did return to Sierra Leone.

trailblazers.name: Yung Wing
trailblazers.text: In 1854 he became the first Chinese student to graduate from an American university, Yale College. He started the Chinese Educational Mission, which brought 120 Chinese students to study in New England, with a headquarters in Hartford built in 1874. He became a U.S. citizen, but the Chinese Exclusion Act later took that status away.

trailblazers.name: Gladys Tantaquidgeon
trailblazers.text: Born on the Mohegan Reservation in Uncasville, she trained from age five with Mohegan elder women and later studied anthropology. With her father and brother she started the Tantaquidgeon Museum in 1931. Her careful records helped the Mohegan Tribe win federal recognition in 1994.

landforms: Litchfield Hills (rolling mountains in the northwest)
Mount Frissell's southern slope, the state's highest point (2,379 feet), and Bear Mountain, its highest peak
Connecticut River Valley in the middle of the state
Coastal marshes and beaches along Long Island Sound
geography.regions: Connecticut has hilly uplands in the northwest (the Litchfield Hills) and in the northeast, the wide Connecticut River Valley through the middle where most people live, and a low coast of marshes, beaches and harbors along Long Island Sound.

ecosystems.name: Long Island Sound estuary
ecosystems.about: Long Island Sound is an estuary where fresh river water mixes with salt water, giving feeding, nesting and nursery grounds to many plants and animals; it was named an Estuary of National Significance in 1988. In late summer, low oxygen near the bottom can harm sea life.

ecosystems.name: Connecticut River tidal marshes
ecosystems.about: The Connecticut River has an internationally important group of tidal fresh, brackish and salt marshes. Shad, salmon, herring and other fish that travel between salt and fresh water use its rivers and streams.

ecosystems.name: Oak and New England forests
ecosystems.about: Oak forests grow in the south and upland New England forests in the northwest. Mountain laurel, the state flower, grows on low ridges, and Atlantic white cedar grows in southern wetlands.

science.weather: Connecticut has four seasons: hot, humid summers and cold winters with snow in the north, and milder winters on the coast. Fast summer thunderstorms bring lightning, and the state averages about one tornado a year. Nor'easters can drop heavy snow, and leftover tropical storms sometimes hit; the 1938 hurricane killed hundreds of people in New England.
science.resources: Connecticut's coast made it a center for shipbuilding, whaling (New London was a top whaling port) and seafood. Today finance and insurance (big insurance companies such as Travelers and The Hartford) and manufacturing, such as jet engines, are big parts of the economy.
science.highlight: Dinosaur tracks! About 2,000 early Jurassic dinosaur footprints, about 200 million years old, were uncovered in Rocky Hill in 1966. At Dinosaur State Park, 500 of them are on view under a geodesic dome and the rest are buried to protect them; it is one of the largest dinosaur track sites in North America. The state fossil is the track called Eubrontes.

g3_ss.title: Connecticut's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find Hartford, learn what the governor and General Assembly do, discover why towns (not counties) run local government, and read Article First, Section 20 of the state constitution.

g3_ss.title: Connecticut's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Pequot, Mohegan and river nations of long ago, learn about wampum and the Three Sisters crops, and meet the five tribal nations of Connecticut today.

g3_ss.title: Connecticut Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Meet Venture Smith, Prudence Crandall and Sarah Harris, Yung Wing and Gladys Tantaquidgeon, and ask what new path each one opened.

g45_ss.title: Connecticut's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Compare Pequot, Mohegan and river nations before 1614, using wampum, village life and the Mohegan and Pequot museums' own stories as evidence.

g45_ss.title: Colonial Connecticut: Colonies, the Pequot War and the Fundamental Orders
g45_ss.plan: Trace Dutch and English arrival, the Pequot War and Treaty of Hartford, and the Fundamental Orders and 1662 Charter, asking who gained and who lost.

g45_ss.title: Connecticut 1784–1877: Slow Freedom
g45_ss.plan: Study gradual emancipation (1784), statehood (1788), Venture Smith, Prudence Crandall, the Amistad case, the end of slavery in 1848, the 29th Connecticut (Colored) Infantry and Yung Wing's Chinese Educational Mission.

g3_sci.title: Long Island Sound: Where Rivers Meet the Sea
g3_sci.plan: Learn what an estuary is, meet oysters, shad and shorebirds, and test how fresh and salt water mix.

g3_sci.title: Dinosaur Tracks of Connecticut
g3_sci.plan: Visit the Rocky Hill trackway (virtually), measure footprints like Eubrontes, and learn how tracks became fossils.

g3_sci.title: Four Seasons and Storms
g3_sci.plan: Chart Connecticut's seasons and learn how families get ready for nor'easters, thunderstorms and hurricanes.

g45_sci.title: Connecticut Ecosystems: Sound, Marsh and Forest
g45_sci.plan: Compare Long Island Sound, Connecticut River tidal marshes and oak forests, and build a food web for each.

g45_sci.title: Keeping Long Island Sound Healthy
g45_sci.plan: Use oxygen data to explain late-summer low-oxygen zones in the Sound and how people work to reduce pollution.

g45_sci.title: Rocks, Rifts and Dinosaur Tracks
g45_sci.plan: Use Dinosaur State Park's early Jurassic tracks (about 2,000 found, 500 on view) to explain how scientists read fossils to learn how dinosaurs lived and moved.
